title: The Shew-Stone and the Four Thousand Books: Dee from Mortlake to Bohemia and back
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Tower Ward and the Flying Beetle

stops.name: London, Tower Ward: the mercer's son
stops.date_confidence: attested; the day and hour are given by Dee himself in his own horoscope
stops.campa: A son is born to Rowland Dee, mercer, in the parish of Tower ward, within sight of the river traffic that carries English cloth to Antwerp. The father is Welsh and holds a small place about the court of Henry VIII; the mother is Johanna Wild. He will grow up between a warehouse and a palace, in the generation that watches the monasteries broken open and their libraries sold off by the cartload for wrapping paper. Dee gives the day and the hour himself, in his own nativity figure. No record names the house, and no record names the street.
suggested_refs: The parish of Tower ward, London, as recorded in Dee's own nativity figure
sources: Wikipedia, 'John Dee' (citing Fell Smith 1909 and Woolley 2012)

stops.name: St John's College, Cambridge: eighteen hours at the desk
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: He comes up at fifteen from the chantry school at Chelmsford and sets himself a rule he will still be quoting fifty years later: eighteen hours a day at his books, four for sleep, two for meals and all the rest of living. Greek, Latin, arithmetic, the doctrine of the spheres. Here he fixes the habit that governs the rest of him, which is to answer a difficulty by reading everything ever written on it and then buying the book. The BA follows in 1545 or early 1546. The term is not recorded, and the two dates sit unresolved in the sources.
suggested_refs: The Chelmsford chantry school, predecessor of the 1551 royal foundation, on a site since lost
sources: Peter French, John Dee: The World of an Elizabethan Magus (1972)

stops.name: Trinity College, Cambridge: the scarabaeus flies to Jupiter's palace
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of the college's foundation; the staging of the Peace is undated within his fellowship
stops.campa: Henry VIII founds Trinity in December and Dee is named among its original fellows, under-reader in Greek at nineteen. For the college performance of the Peace of Aristophanes he builds a mechanical beetle that carries a man and his basket of victuals up to the palace of Jupiter above the stage. The audience talks about it for decades, and some of them decide it was done by an art of another kind. The word conjuror attaches to him then, in a Cambridge hall, thirty-five years before he ever asks an angel anything.
stops.quote: Hereupon I did sett forth ... a Greek comedy of Aristophanes, named in Greek [Eirene], in Latin Pax; with the performance of the Scarabaeus, his flying up to Jupiter's palace, with a man and his basket of victuals on her back
stops.quote_source: John Dee, 'Compendious Rehearsall', quoted in the Dictionary of National Biography, 'Dee, John'
suggested_refs: Trinity College hall, Cambridge, and the flying machine built for Aristophanes' Peace

stops.name: Leuven, the instruments and Gemma Frisius
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: He crosses to the Low Countries and enrolls at the old university of Louvain, where Gemma Frisius teaches the mathematics of position and Gerardus Mercator is cutting plates that will change how Europe pictures itself. Dee is twenty-one and buys what he can carry home: two great globes of Mercator's making, a brass astronomer's staff, two rings of Frisius's design. The instruments go back to England and afterwards onto the desks of the pilots sailing for the north-west. So do the friendships. He and Mercator write to each other for years.
suggested_refs: Mercator's globes and Frisius's rings, brought back from Louvain to England in 1550
sources: French, John Dee: The World of an Elizabethan Magus

stops.name: Paris, Euclid to a hall that will not hold them
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Word of the Englishman from Louvain has gone ahead of him. At twenty-three he lectures without fee on the first book of Euclid at the College de Rheims, and the hall cannot take the crowd; men stand at the windows outside to hear the propositions read. The crowd is Dee's own account of it, and no source gives a number. The French court offers him a stipend to stay. He refuses and goes home to England, where there is no chair of mathematics for anyone to offer him.
suggested_refs: The Euclid lectures at the College de Rheims, Paris, 1550

stops.name: Hampton Court, the charge of calculating
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the proceedings run across several months, month defaulted
stops.campa: Under Mary, two informers denounce him for casting the nativities of the queen, her husband, and the Princess Elizabeth. Calculating is the charge, and it can be pressed into treason, since to compute a sovereign's death is held to be imagining it. He is taken up, held, and examined by the Privy Council over several months. The mathematical case collapses and the Star Chamber clears him of it. The religious case is not dismissed with the rest. It is handed on to a bishop, and the bishop is Edmund Bonner.
suggested_refs: The Privy Council proceedings against Dee for 'lewd and vain practices of calculating and conjuring', 1555

stops.name: Fulham Palace, in Bishop Bonner's house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month inferred from the sequence of the proceedings
stops.campa: Cleared of treason, he is delivered to Edmund Bonner, Bishop of London, to be examined on his faith, and ends by living in Bonner's household as his chaplain through the months when Bonner is sending Protestants to the fire at Smithfield. He took Catholic orders the year before by the bishop's own dispensation, on the seventeenth of February 1554. Three years on he will elect the coronation day of a Protestant queen. What he believed in either year he does not write down anywhere.
suggested_refs: Fulham Palace, residence of Bishop Edmund Bonner, where Dee was examined in 1555

stops.name: Whitehall, the library that is refused
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: He lays before Queen Mary a supplication for the recovery and preservation of ancient writers and monuments: a royal library, and agents sent through the realm to buy or copy what the dissolution of the monasteries has scattered into private hands, grocers' counters, and bakers' ovens. The crown declines, and no reason for the refusal is recorded. Dee undertakes the work himself, on a scholar's income, one purchase at a time. The books go to Mortlake.
suggested_refs: Dee's 1556 supplication to Mary I for a national library of ancient writers and monuments
sources: Julian Roberts and Andrew Watson, John Dee's Library Catalogue (1990)

stops.name: Whitehall, a day chosen for a coronation
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the accession is November 1558 and the coronation follows on 15 January 1559, but the date of the consultation is not recorded
stops.campa: Elizabeth comes to the throne in November and Robert Dudley brings Dee to her to elect the day of the crowning. He works the figures and returns the fifteenth of January. She is crowned on it. From that hour he holds no office and draws no fixed salary, and yet the queen calls him her philosopher and sends for him when comets appear, when she is ill, when she wants to know what right in law she has to the far side of the ocean. The arrangement makes him famous and keeps him poor. Where the consultation happened, and on what day, nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The election of 15 January 1559 as the coronation date of Elizabeth I

stops.name: Antwerp, ten days of copying
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: On a book-buying journey he is lent a manuscript of the Steganographia of Johannes Trithemius, the abbot of Sponheim who set down the names of the planetary angels and the hours of their governance and was called a necromancer for it. Everything that comes twenty years later at Mortlake, the angelic names, the tables, the calls, has its grammar in this abbot's cipher manual. Dee copies the whole of it by hand in ten days, in a borrowed room. He reckons those ten days' work worth a thousand crowns to him, and says so.
stops.quote: I wrote out the boke Steganographia ... which in ten dayes I did
stops.quote_source: Dee's diary, quoted in Fell Smith, John Dee (1909)
suggested_refs: Dee's holograph copy of Trithemius's Steganographia, made at Antwerp in ten days

stops.name: Antwerp, the Monas printed by Willem Silvius
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of printing; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: He writes the Monas Hieroglyphica in twelve days and Willem Silvius prints it, dedicated to the Emperor Maximilian II: twenty-four theorems on a single composite glyph built out of the signs of the moon, the sun, the elements, and fire, which Dee holds to contain the unity of the heavens and the whole alchemical work at once. The symbol outlives every explanation given of it, including his. Readers then and since have called it impenetrable. Elizabeth asks him to expound it to her, and he obliges.
suggested_refs: The 1564 Antwerp first edition of the Monas Hieroglyphica, printed by Willem Silvius

stops.name: Mortlake, the house opposite the church
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: He settles his household at Mortlake on the Thames, in a house facing the parish church, and begins knocking rooms together to hold the books. At its height the library runs to some four thousand printed volumes and hundreds of manuscripts, larger than what Oxford or Cambridge then held. In the outbuildings there are laboratories, and a store of instruments, globes, and sea charts. Courtiers, sea captains, and foreign scholars come upriver to use it, and are put up in the house while they read.
suggested_refs: The site of Dee's house at Mortlake, opposite St Mary the Virgin, later the Mortlake tapestry works
sources: Roberts and Watson, John Dee's Library Catalogue (1990)

stops.name: London, the Mathematicall Praeface
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Henry Billingsley englishes Euclid and Dee writes the preface to it, fifty folio pages arguing that mathematics stands in the middle between the divine and the material, and setting out a whole tree of arts grown from that root: perspective, astronomy, music, cosmography, navigation, and the art he names archemastrie. He writes it for shipwrights, surveyors, and instrument makers who have no Latin, and for a century afterwards it is the manifesto of English practical mathematics. Of all sciences, he tells them, next to theology this one is most diuine, most pure, most ample and generall.
stops.quote: Of all Sciences, next to Theologie, it is most diuine, most pure, most ample and generall
stops.quote_source: John Dee, 'Mathematicall Praeface' to Henry Billingsley's English Euclid (1570)
suggested_refs: The 1570 Billingsley Euclid with Dee's Mathematicall Praeface
sources: John Dee, 'Mathematicall Praeface' (1570), Project Gutenberg ed. 22062

stops.name: Mortlake, the letter to Burghley
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He writes to Lord Burghley to set down plainly what twenty years of study have earned him: two small church livings, no place at court, no pension, and a house full of books bought with money he did not have. He is forty-seven. The letter asks for leave to search for treasure trove, and for some settled provision. In it he claims that this land never bred any man whose account in learning can be proved greater than his own. It is the first of the petitions. There will be thirty more years of them.
stops.quote: in zeale to the best lerning and knowledg, and in incredible toyle of body and mynde, very many yeres, therfore onely endured, I know most assuredly that this land never bred any man, whose account therein can evidently be proved greater than myne
stops.quote_source: Dee to Lord Burghley, 3 October 1574, quoted in the Dictionary of National Biography, 'Dee, John'
suggested_refs: Dee's letter to Lord Burghley of 3 October 1574, the first of his petitions for provision

stops.name: Mortlake, the Queen at the church wall
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; 16 March 1574 by the English year beginning 25 March, 1575 by modern reckoning, and the sources give both
stops.campa: The queen rides to Mortlake meaning to see the library. Dee's wife Katherine has been carried out of the house for burial four hours before, and Elizabeth will not go in. Instead she sends for his famous glass, the convex mirror that shrinks and reverses whatever stands before it, and the Earl of Leicester lifts her down from her horse at the church wall. She wills him to fetch the glass and to show unto her some of the properties of it, which he does, standing in the road outside his own gate on the day of the burial.
stops.quote: her Majestie refused to come in; but willed to fetch my glass so famous, and to show unto her some of the properties of it, which I did
stops.quote_source: Dee, 'Compendious Memorial', quoted in the editorial notes to The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, ed. J. O. Halliwell (Camden Society, 1842)
suggested_refs: The churchyard wall of St Mary the Virgin, Mortlake, where Leicester handed the queen down
sources: Halliwell (ed.), The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee (1842)

stops.name: Ratcliff, the pilots for the north-west passage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month inferred from the sailing season of Frobisher's first voyage
stops.campa: At the Thames-side yards at Ratcliff he teaches Martin Frobisher's masters and pilots the use of the compass of variation and of his own paradoxal compass, drawn for the high latitudes where an ordinary chart fails. In the same years he is arguing in print, in the General and Rare Memorials Pertayning to the Perfect Arte of Navigation, for a standing royal navy and for the queen's title to the northern and western lands. He never sails himself; he supplies the maps and the claim. The phrase he puts into English for the idea is the British Empire.
suggested_refs: General and Rare Memorials Pertayning to the Perfect Arte of Navigation (1577)

segments.name: The Queen's Conjuror and the Shew-Stone

stops.name: Windsor Castle, reading the comet
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year and to the appearance of the comet in November; the days at Windsor are not separately dated
stops.campa: A comet hangs over England in November and the court is frightened by it. The queen sends for Dee and he attends her at Windsor to say what it means. By now he is the crown's standing interpreter of the sky and of anything else that will not explain itself: an eclipse, a new star, an ill dream of the queen's, a wax image of her found with a pin in its breast. He is sent for each time, and each time rides home to Mortlake unpaid. What he told her about the comet nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The great comet of 1577, read at Windsor before Elizabeth I

stops.name: Mortlake, the glove pulled off at the gate
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The queen rides past his garden with the court behind her, stops in the field beside it and stands a good while, then comes into the street at the great gate. Dee is at his door making his obeisance. She beckons him with her hand and he comes to the side of her coach. He writes it down that night in the margin of his almanac, in the clipped mixture of Latin and English his diary is kept in, where sixty years of a life go by in phrases of five words: she very speedily pulled off her glove and gave me her hand to kiss.
stops.quote: she very speedily pulled off her glove and gave me her hand to kiss
stops.quote_source: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, entry of 17 September 1580, ed. J. O. Halliwell
suggested_refs: Dee's annotated almanacs, in which the private diary was written
sources: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, ed. Halliwell, Project Gutenberg 19553

stops.name: Richmond Palace, two rolls of the Queen's title
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He carries to Richmond two great rolls setting out the queen's title to lands beyond the ocean, drawn from Welsh chronicle, from the voyage of Madoc, from the northern conquests ascribed to King Arthur. The argument is that a queen may claim what her forebears reached, and that Englishmen and Welshmen reached further, earlier, than anyone had troubled to write down. It is a legal case for empire made out of national legend, and the lawyers will go on refining it for a century after he is dead. Elizabeth takes the rolls from him in the garden at Richmond.
stops.quote: I delivered my two rolls of the Quene's Majesties title unto herself in the garden at Richemond
stops.quote_source: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, entry of 3 October 1580, ed. J. O. Halliwell
suggested_refs: Dee's rolls of the queen's title, and the manuscript Brytannicae reipublicae synopsis
sources: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, ed. Halliwell, Project Gutenberg 19553

stops.name: Mortlake, Edward Kelley at the table of practice
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: A young man giving the name Edward Talbot presents himself at Mortlake. He has no ears, having lost them in a pillory, and he keeps his cap on indoors. Dee has spent years praying to be shown things and has seen nothing at all; the scryers he has tried before were frauds or worse. The partnership begun this afternoon will run seven years and cross Europe. This one sits down to the crystal shew-stone on the table of practice, above the great wax seal called the Sigillum Dei Aemeth, and almost at once is describing an angel and giving its name.
suggested_refs: The Sigillum Dei Aemeth and the wax seals of Dee's table of practice, British Museum
sources: Deborah Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels (1999)

stops.name: Westminster, the book for the correction of the calendar
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Rome has cut ten days out of the year and England has not. Dee is asked for the arithmetic and delivers to the Lord Treasurer a treatise proposing that England drop eleven days, correcting to the birth of Christ rather than to the Council of Nicaea, with the loss arranged to fall where it will hurt trade least. Burghley is satisfied. The astronomers are satisfied. The bishops will not take a calendar from the pope, and England keeps the old reckoning for another hundred and seventy years.
stops.quote: I delivered my boke to the Lord Threasorer for the correction of the Calender
stops.quote_source: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, entry of 26 February 1583, ed. J. O. Halliwell
suggested_refs: Dee's 1583 treatise on the reformation of the calendar, submitted to Lord Burghley
sources: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, ed. Halliwell, Project Gutenberg 19553

stops.name: Mortlake, Albert Laski and the leaving of England
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: Albert Laski, Palatine of Sieradz, arrives in England trailing debts and a reputation for magnificence, and the queen hands him on to Dee to be entertained and impressed. In the shew-stone the angels tell Laski he will be king of Poland. In September Dee packs what he can carry, leaves the house and the four thousand books in the keeping of other men, and goes down the river by night with his wife, three children, Kelley, Kelley's wife, and the Polish prince. He is fifty-six years old. He will be gone six years.
suggested_refs: The night departure from Mortlake, September 1583, with the Laski party
sources: Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels

stops.name: Lask, the Palatine's house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month inferred from the length of the overland journey
stops.campa: The party reaches Laski's own town after months of roads, ferries, and Lutheran innkeepers, and settles into a patron's house whose promised revenues turn out to be mortgaged twice over. The angels have opinions about Polish politics now, and about which prince should hold which crown. The sessions go on unaltered in the new room: prayer, fasting, the stone, Kelley reporting what he sees, Dee writing all of it down in books that a later owner will hide under the false bottom of a chest.
suggested_refs: Laski's seat at Lask, first station of the continental years
sources: Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels
R. J. W. Evans, Rudolf II and His World (1973)

stops.name: Krakow, the forty-eight Keys
stops.date_confidence: attested to Krakow and to about a year after the March 1583 alphabet visions; the reception straddles 1583 and 1584 and the month is not fixed
stops.campa: In lodgings at Krakow, over weeks of daily sessions, Kelley receives the forty-eight Angelic Keys: verses in a language with its own alphabet and its own syntax, dictated backwards letter by letter so that the words should not take effect while they were being written. Dee sets them down as they come and then copies them again in their true order. He calls the tongue Celestial Speech; later ages call it Enochian, after the patriarch who walked with God and was not. Whether Kelley invented it, and how a man invents a syntax backwards, is still open.
suggested_refs: The Claves Angelicae, the forty-eight Enochian Keys received at Krakow
sources: Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels

stops.name: Prague Castle, the warning delivered to Rudolf II
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month traditional
stops.campa: Admitted at last to Rudolf II, Dee tells the emperor of the Romans to his face that the angel of the Lord has appeared to him, that Rudolf's sins are known, and that if he will hear and repent he shall conquer the Turk. It is not the language in which emperors are addressed. Rudolf, who collects clockmakers, cabalists, and gold-makers and who is in no hurry about any of them, receives the Englishman courteously. Access afterwards runs through secretaries, and then through nobody. Nothing at all follows from the audience.
suggested_refs: The audience chambers of Hradcany under Rudolf II
sources: Evans, Rudolf II and His World

stops.name: Charles Square, Prague: the house that carries another man's name
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the tradition is not dated and attaches to no document, year defaulted to the middle of the Bohemian years
stops.campa: The house on Charles Square carries the name of Johann Faust, whose bargain the town says was settled there through a hole in the roof that no plaster will close. Within a generation Dee and Kelley are folded into the same story: the foreign scholars at the emperor's court, the furnaces going at night, the language nobody else can read. In this city, in these years, men were trying to make gold and to get speech out of the dark, and the town put the two Englishmen at this address. No document does. The tradition carries no date and attaches to no paper at all.
suggested_refs: The Faust House on Karlovo namesti, Prague, and its accreted legends
sources: Evans, Rudolf II and His World
Prague civic tradition, recorded in local guidebooks

stops.name: Prague, six days to leave the Emperor's lands
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month inferred, and the separate summons before the nuncio Malaspina is dated 27 March 1587 in the sources
stops.campa: The papal nuncio has read reports of the angelic conferences, calls the doctrine in them heretical, and there is talk of sending both Englishmen to Rome. Rudolf, who wants no quarrel with the Curia over two foreigners, orders them out of the imperial lands within six days. In under two years Dee has gone from an imperial audience to a deportation order. They go inside the six days, with the books and the stone and the wives and the children, to Bohemian noblemen less afraid of nuncios than the emperor is.
suggested_refs: The nunciature of Germanico Malaspina at Prague and the expulsion order against Dee and Kelley
sources: Evans, Rudolf II and His World

stops.name: Trebon, the powder projected
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in Kelley's sources; the transmutation itself is reported, not verified
stops.campa: Under the protection of Vilem of Rozmberk the party settles in the castle at Trebon, where a laboratory is fitted out for them. On the nineteenth of December Kelley projects a powder onto base metal and produces, before witnesses, what is taken for gold. From that day the emperor's men want Kelley, and the Bohemian lords want Kelley, and the man left holding the notebooks is the old mathematician who brought him out of England. Dee enters the transmutation in his diary without comment.
suggested_refs: The laboratory at Trebon castle, seat of Vilem of Rozmberk
sources: Evans, Rudolf II and His World

stops.name: Trebon, all things in common
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of the covenant; the actions of that spring run 4 April to 23 May 1587
stops.campa: In the actions of that spring the spirit in the stone commands the two households to hold all things in common, wives included. Dee writes that he is grieved to the heart and that the thing is against the law of God; Kelley says he will have no more to do with the actions at all. Within weeks the covenant is drawn up and subscribed by all four of them. A son is born to Jane Dee the following February and christened Theodore, gift of God. The sources name the angel Uriel in one place and Madimi in another.
stops.quote: I, John Dee, Edward Kelley, and our two wives, covenanted with God, and subscribed the same, for indissoluble and inviolable unities, charity, and friendship keeping between us four; and all things between us to be common.
stops.quote_source: Dee's spiritual diary, entry of 3 May 1587, quoted in the Dictionary of National Biography, 'Dee, John'
suggested_refs: The manuscript of the third action, 4 April to 23 May 1587, and the subscribed covenant
sources: Meric Casaubon (ed.), A True and Faithful Relation (1659)

stops.name: Trebon, the hand given in charity
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: A year on, the two households are barely speaking. Kelley by then is riding often between Trebon and Prague, and the furnace work is his alone. Then, at the sacrament, Kelley's wife gives her hand in charity to Dee and to Jane. It is the last reconciliation the diary records between the four of them, and what any of them made of that spring afterwards nobody set down. The entry runs: Mistris Kelly received the sacrament, and to me and my wife gave her hand in charity; and we rushed not from her.
stops.quote: Mistris Kelly received the sacrament, and to me and my wife gave her hand in charity; and we rushed not from her.
stops.quote_source: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, entry of 22 May 1588, ed. J. O. Halliwell
suggested_refs: Dee's diary entries for the Trebon years, 1586 to 1589
sources: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, ed. Halliwell, Project Gutenberg 19553

stops.name: Trebon, the glass handed over
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the place of the entry is not stated in the diary and is inferred from Dee's residence
stops.campa: On the fourth of December Dee gives Kelley the glass: the stone he has kept since 1582, which the queen of England and the emperor of the Romans have both been shown. He is handing over the instrument and with it the work. In six years the angels have never once spoken to him directly, and now the man they speak through will keep the stone as his own. Within months Dee is packing for England and Kelley is riding to Prague to make gold for Rudolf.
stops.quote: I gave to Mr. Ed. Kelley my Glass, so highly and long estemed of, our Quene, and the Emperor Randolph the second
stops.quote_source: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, entry of 4 December 1588, ed. J. O. Halliwell
suggested_refs: The shew-stone, its later ownership disputed between Dee's and Kelley's descendants
sources: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, ed. Halliwell, Project Gutenberg 19553

stops.name: Bremen, Khunrath at the door
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Waiting at Bremen through most of 1589 for money, passports, and a ship, Dee keeps a scholar's open house in rented rooms. On the twenty-seventh of May the physician Heinrich Khunrath comes to see him, and afterwards writes the Amphitheatre of Eternal Wisdom with its engraving of a chamber that is oratory and laboratory at once, a man kneeling between an altar and a furnace. The Landgrave of Hesse sends his own doctor to the rented rooms as well. He has no library now, no patron, and no fixed country, and he is still the man everyone wants an hour with. Khunrath's book is printed at Hamburg in 1595.
suggested_refs: Heinrich Khunrath's Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae, first printed at Hamburg in 1595

stops.name: Stade, waiting for a man who does not come
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of the diary entry
stops.campa: He has spent the best part of a year getting from Bohemia to a ship: the roads, Bremen, borrowed money, letters that go unanswered. He comes down at last to Stade on the Elbe, where the English Merchant Adventurers keep their staple, and writes in the diary that he hopes to meet Mr. Edward Kelly there. Kelley does not come. The two men who spent seven years in one room writing down the speech of angels never see each other again. Dee takes ship on the nineteenth of November.
suggested_refs: The Merchant Adventurers' staple at Stade on the lower Elbe
sources: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, ed. Halliwell, Project Gutenberg 19553

stops.name: Mortlake, the house found open
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; he came into the Thames at Gravesend on 2 December and first slept at Mortlake on 25 December
stops.campa: He comes into the Thames at Gravesend on the second of December and does not sleep in his own house until Christmas night. What he finds there has been going on for six years: books sold, lent, and carried off by the men he trusted with them, some hundreds of volumes gone, the great mirror broken, the laboratory glass smashed, the quadrant destroyed. He spends years afterward drawing up inventories of what he owned and petitioning to be paid for it. A few volumes come back. Most do not.
suggested_refs: Roberts and Watson's reconstruction of Dee's library catalogue and of the 1583-89 dispersal
sources: Roberts and Watson, John Dee's Library Catalogue (1990)

stops.name: Mortlake, I thank thee, Dee
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day and the hour
stops.campa: The queen passes his door again at half past three in the afternoon and he meets her at the Eastsheen gate. She puts down her mask and speaks to him with a merry face about a promise: she had sent him a hundred angels, the gold coin stamped with the archangel Michael, and it had not been enough to keep him, and both of them know it. He writes the words down that night. In the same years he writes that he has sold his plate and is borrowing on the furniture.
stops.quote: I thank thee, Dee; there was never promisse made but it was broken or kept.
stops.quote_source: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, entry of 4 December 1590, ed. J. O. Halliwell
suggested_refs: The Eastsheen gate at Mortlake, on the queen's road to Richmond
sources: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, ed. Halliwell, Project Gutenberg 19553

stops.name: Isleworth, a wife and seven children before the Queen
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He brings his wife and seven children to stand in front of Elizabeth at Isleworth. It is a petition made of bodies: here is the household, here is what the philosopher of England has to feed on nothing. He has been asking for a place for years and has been answered with promises, and with commissions of inquiry into his losses. The following year the crown will find him a post four days' ride to the north, in a town he has never seen. The whole of the day goes into the diary in eleven words: I, my wife, and seven children, before the Quene at Thisellworth.
stops.quote: I, my wife, and seven children, before the Quene at Thisellworth
stops.quote_source: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, entry of 3 June 1594, ed. J. O. Halliwell
suggested_refs: The royal manor at Isleworth, where Dee presented his household in 1594
sources: The Private Diary of Dr. John Dee, ed. Halliwell, Project Gutenberg 19553

stops.name: Manchester, the warden nobody obeys
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month inferred
stops.campa: The wardenship of Christ's College, Manchester, is what the crown finally gives him: a decayed collegiate foundation with disputed revenues, fellows who cheat him over the rents and despise him openly, and a town that fetches him out to examine children said to be possessed. The revenues are in other men's hands and the accounts do not add up. He is sixty-eight when he takes it. He rides north with his family and his surviving books and holds the office, in name at least, until the day he dies.
suggested_refs: Christ's College, Manchester, later Chetham's, and the warden's lodgings

stops.name: Manchester, Jane in the collegiate church
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of March, but the year is given as 1604 in some sources and 1605 in others, an Old Style and New Style split on a March date
stops.campa: Plague comes to Manchester and Jane Dee dies of it in March, after thirty years of marriage, six years of exile, and eight children. She is buried in the collegiate church. Others of the household go the same way in the same visitation. Dee is near eighty, warden of a college he cannot govern, in a northern town in a plague year. Word reaches him in these years, if it has not before, that Kelley died a prisoner in Bohemia, of injuries got climbing out of a tower window.
suggested_refs: Manchester Cathedral, then the collegiate church, burial place of Jane Dee

stops.name: Mortlake, the books sold one at a time
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the return south is dated 1605 and the last years are undated, year defaulted
stops.campa: He comes back south to the house at Mortlake that he can no longer keep up, and lives there with his daughter Katherine, selling one book at a time to buy food. He is past eighty. Katherine keeps the house and does the fetching. People still come to the door to have figures cast for them, and he still casts them for whatever they can pay. The library that scholars crossed the Channel to consult is going out of the house a volume at a time, in whatever order the buyers happen to want.
suggested_refs: The dispersal of the last of the Mortlake library, sold piecemeal in Dee's final years

stops.name: St Mary the Virgin, Mortlake: the chancel with no stone
stops.date_confidence: unknown within a window; death falls between December 1608 and March 1609, and neither the parish register nor the gravestone survives to fix it
stops.campa: He dies in the house opposite the church, about eighty-one years old, and is buried inside it, beneath the chancel floor. The parish register for those months is lost. The gravestone, if there was one, is gone. Nobody set down the day, and nobody set down the spot beneath the floor either. A man who spent his life fixing dates, who told a queen which day to be crowned on and a treasurer which eleven days England ought to drop out of the year, has no date of his own.
suggested_refs: The chancel of St Mary the Virgin, Mortlake, and the lost parish register of 1608-09

stops.name: Kassel, the Monas on the wedding invitation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the Chymical Wedding; the manifesto wave runs 1614 to 1616
stops.campa: The manifestos come off the German presses in three years: the Fama in 1614, the Confessio in 1615, and in 1616 the Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreutz, whose invitation to the royal wedding opens with a symbol. The symbol is the composite glyph of the Monas Hieroglyphica, Dee's own mark, set on the door of a brotherhood that may never have existed at all. He has been dead seven years and is not consulted; the sign travels without the man. No evidence has ever been found that he belonged to any secret order, in his lifetime or before it.
suggested_refs: The Fama Fraternitatis (1614), Confessio (1615), and Chymical Wedding (1616)

stops.name: London, A True and Faithful Relation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Meric Casaubon prints the spiritual diaries entire, under the title A True and Faithful Relation of What Passed for Many Yeers Between Dr. John Dee and Some Spirits. The book is meant to shame the enthusiasts of its own decade, and it fixes Dee's name for three centuries as a warning; it also puts every word of the conferences into print, where anyone at all can find them and try them. Casaubon's preface argues that Dee was an honest and learned man deceived by devils.
suggested_refs: Meric Casaubon, A True and Faithful Relation (London, 1659)
sources: Meric Casaubon (ed.), A True and Faithful Relation (1659)

stops.name: Bloomsbury, the black mirror and the wax seal
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the date of Lord Frederick Campbell's visit to Horace Walpole is not recorded, and the year given here stands for Walpole's ownership
stops.campa: A disc of polished black obsidian, cut in Mexico before the conquest and carried to Europe in the late 1520s among the loot, comes to Horace Walpole, who is told it was Dr. Dee's speculum and labels it so. Dee's own writings never mention such a mirror; his instrument was a crystal. Every later picture of him puts the obsidian into his hand anyway. The disc lies now in the British Museum beside the wax Sigillum Dei Aemeth, the seals from the table of practice, a gold amulet, and a crystal globe six centimetres across.
suggested_refs: The Aztec obsidian mirror, the Sigillum Dei Aemeth, and the shew-stone in the British Museum
sources: British Museum collection records, cited in Wikipedia, 'John Dee'
Antiquity (2021), geochemical sourcing of the obsidian mirror

stops.name: London, the tablets taken up again
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1893 for the Kelley edition; Mathers's Enochian work dates from the 1880s
stops.campa: Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers has been reading the angelic manuscripts in the British Museum and builds the tablets, the keys, and the names into the working curriculum of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, whose members go so far as to invent a chess played on four elemental boards drawn from the tablets. Three hundred years on, in rented rooms in London, the calls are being read aloud again. Arthur Edward Waite brings out an English edition of the alchemical writings of Edward Kelley in the same decade, in 1893.
suggested_refs: The Alchemical Writings of Edward Kelly, ed. A. E. Waite (London, 1893)

stops.name: Mortlake, the plaque on the wall
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of the unveiling
stops.campa: Four hundred and four years after he was put under the floor without a marker, a memorial to Dee is unveiled inside the church at Mortlake. It does not mark the grave, because nobody knows where under the chancel the grave is. His house across the road became the Mortlake tapestry works, and at the end of the eighteenth century a girls' school, and after that nothing at all; there is no address left in the village to point at. The plaque is the nearest thing to a headstone he has ever had.
suggested_refs: The 2013 memorial to John Dee inside St Mary the Virgin, Mortlake
